utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good morning, counsel. Excuse me, but I think we have a problem with the translation. I'm on channel 4, and I'm getting the Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One, two, three. Is that all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-A, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. As you know, we are here today to have a short Status Conference in order to plan for the oral argument which will take place on July 23rd, through July 25th. I hope that by our work today, we will be able to make that hearing more expeditious and more fruitful for all concerned. I think for the record, we will have counsel identify themselves. I'll begin with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour. Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution, with Ms. Sonja Boelaert-Suominen, and Ms. Norul Rashid. I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We'll begin with the Defence counsel. Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Slokovic-Glumac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Anthony Abell appearing again on behalf of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I represent Mr. Drago Josipovic for today's hearing. I'm working with Mr. Clegg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And you are Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Charbit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation] THE REPORTER: There is no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There's a problem with the English interpretation, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say, I'm on channel 4, as Your Honour was, and I'm not getting any English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Neither am I. I'm just listening to the voices. Well, Madam Registrar, can you check on this and see if we can get the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes, I can. All right. Thank you. That was very speedy. I thought that we would do three things today, that one, we would have a brief summary of where we are with respect to any outstanding briefs or motions; two, we will make an oral ruling on the motion for judicial notice under 94; and finally, we will discuss how the forthcoming argument will be conducted. Let me begin then by just bringing us up-to-date. Mr. Radovic, do you have something? What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of my colleague, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac and in my own name, I would like to say the following to the Honourable Court: The submission of the Prosecutor that was filed in response to our own motion we received only today. We could not take it before because it was waiting for us at our locker here. Our colleague Mr. Pavkovic was supposed to travel to The Hague, and during that trip he was supposed to take the documents that were there. However, the Registry did not allow him to travel. Since we received this only today, we would have the right to look into it for 15 days. However, we took a look at it today, and however -- about 200 pages referred to our clients, in English. However, since English is not our mother tongue, we have to have all of this translated into Croat. We have to study it and then reply and then have the reply translated into English, and we are not in a position to do that within 15 days, as is the deadline set by Rule 113. Also, with due respect to the Court, perhaps it was a bit premature to schedule the appeals hearing, because according to Rule 114, the appeals hearing is scheduled only when all time limits expire for filing the briefs provided for in Rules 111, 112, and 113. However, we don't want to turn this into an issue. Nevertheless, in view of the quantity of pages in English concerned and the need to have it all translated into Croatian and then have our own reply translated into English, we would like the appeals hearing to be postponed and we would like to be given at least 30 days in order to submit a proper reply; otherwise this is impossible for us. Actually, the Prosecutor's reply mainly deals with our clients, and that's what makes it so important.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would just like to add the following: Together with this brief, there is also a book of authorities which has 400 pages. So in addition to analysing everything from the brief, we also have to look into the documents that were attached to it. We don't know who made this mistake and we don't know why this happened. However, we are in a position to have to carry out such a voluminous task within eight days, and as my colleague said, it is virtually impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I've heard what you say. I would answer you this way: I certainly will relay your thoughts and your request to my colleagues, who are not here today, but basically, we have scheduled this oral argument for months in advance. We also made it very clear that the Prosecution's brief was due on the date that it was in actually filed, which I believe was June 28th. I understand that because of its voluminous nature, it was not able to be, I believe, faxed - is that true, Madam Registrar? - and it was put in the mailboxes here. Some of the counsel did get it, in fact; others did not. Some of the counsel made that fact that they had not gotten it known to the chief legal officer on the case, Mr. von Hebel. In answer to that, an understanding that there had been this delay of some sorts and that counsel who did not get the brief had made that known to Mr. von Hebel, the Appeals Chamber agreed that the defendants' replies to that Prosecution's brief would not be due until July 18th, which is about ten days from now. As of now, I'm going to proceed with the rest of this hearing on the assumption that -- and I think you should too - that July 18th will be the date. I point out to you that all the Defence counsel have filed their own appellant's brief months ago. They've also filed a supplementary brief. What is due now are the reply briefs to the Prosecution's briefs. Those are by their nature much more brief and they're also by their nature purely responsive to the Prosecution's briefs. They are not the original case made out by the appellant. Although I certainly will relay this request of yours, I myself would not grant it, and I will proceed for the rest of this time on the assumption that by July 18th the Defence counsel would be able to file a response brief to the Prosecution's filing. Many of the Defence counsel did, in fact, get their briefs from the box, and many of them who had some question about -- not many of them, but some who had questions about it called Mr. von Hebel and found out what the adjustment that we made in the time span is. I think it's fair to say that nobody wishes to postpone the argument here and the completion of the trial schedule. I will, however, Mr. Radovic, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, relay your request. If my colleagues do not agree with me, you will be promptly notified, but I do not think that you should count on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Just before we move from that topic, could I just check one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: On the 18th of July, to make sure we're quite clear, the deadline is 4.00 p.m., as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That would be true, would it not, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's all right. I will now go back to the schedule that we had and that I will assume will continue unless the Appeals Chamber decides otherwise, and that would say that we wish to point out to Mr. Josipovic's counsel that we did receive his reply to the Prosecution's amended brief on the 8th. I think the 8th. Anyway, it was Friday, whatever it was. And there was some minor confusion there, but the Appeals Chamber will accept this brief even though there was some delay from the original date that it was due.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's right. It was received by Mr. Clegg on Thursday when he was here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: And he was -- he passed it to me on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we will receive that and take it into consideration. I also wish to point to you July 17th as being the date in one of our orders when copies of the public brief would be due so that anything confidential would be separated out and filed separately. That's, I think, necessary so that both counsel in oral argument may refer -- know what they can refer to freely without asking for any special private sessions, and also so that the Court has an easy reference point when it comes time to read the judgement, to know what's in the public brief and what's not. In that respect, I would ask the Prosecution whether they plan to file a public brief within approximately the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, just before we move from that topic, could I make the suggestion - I hope it's a helpful one -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the dates for the response to the Prosecution's reply to our amended appellant's brief is 18th of July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- it might be easier for us, all of whom are now working to a tight timetable, if the date for the service of the public appellant's brief were that same date, the 18th. It would mean a day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. I understand. I think that's a very reasonable suggestion, and I will grant that on the spot here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So it will be the same date, July 18th, when both of these sets of the public briefs and the replies will be due.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, I have one other date here, and that was for the Prosecution's reply to Mr. Josipovic and Mr. Santic's response to their amended brief, and that I have down as July 19th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say on behalf of Mr. Josipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: -- that we would be grateful if that would be filed by the Prosecution by 2.00 p.m. on July 19th. It's a time table that we have discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Is that possible, Mr. Yapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Then it shall be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Those are the deadlines, barring any change. I don't think anybody should rely on there being any change, but Mr. Radovic and Ms. Slokovic-Glumac's requests will certainly be relayed. Let me go over very briefly the status of all outstanding motions in the case. There is one pending Rule 115 motion of Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic for the admission of a document which was filed some few weeks ago. It's been replied to by the Prosecution. You will receive a written decision on that motion. It will be filed either today or possibly tomorrow, but that motion will be taken care of. We also have some motions of Mr. Josipovic and Vlatko Kupreskic for access to transcripts in the Kordic case, and there may be one in the Blaskic case. What I want to relate to you is that those motions, procedurally, are in the President's office. We are working with them to get an answer from the President, who must make that decision, and as far as any adjustment of schedule afterwards, if those motions are granted, we will take that up as it comes to us, but we are working with the President's office to get those out as soon as we can. Now, I am told but have not yet received that there were two Rule 115 motions which were filed on Thursday or Friday, but anyway within, but just within the deadline of 15 days before the hearing. I have not received those motions yet. When I do, we will try to take care of those as quickly as possible, especially to have them decided before the oral argument. I solicit the Prosecution's cooperation in that respect. I don't know what they are yet, maybe the Prosecution doesn't either, but to the extent that it would be able to reply ahead of the normal deadline, that would be most helpful so that all of those motions can be decided before the oral argument. Now, I would like to take up -- Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic have filed a motion, that the Prosecution has replied to, for judicial notice under Rule 94(A) for a meteorological report from an official Sarajevo weather station about the time at which the sun rose in Sarajevo and Vitez on the morning of April 16th. With the assent of my colleagues, I am going to rule on that motion at this time. So the oral ruling will be the definitive ruling. After consultation and after receiving the reply of the Prosecution, the Appellate Chamber declines to take judicial notice of the report for the following reasons: The report is a piece of additional evidence on a much disputed issue that was litigated at trial, that is, the conditions of visibility in the morning of April 16, 1993. The Trial Court heard much evidence and much testimony on this particular issue. The Appellate Chamber also made a decisions declining several petitioners' requests to admit additional evidence on this topic in the form of videos, because it ruled that such evidence was not unavailable at the trial and so did not meet the first prong of Rule 115. Now, although we are well aware that Rule 94(A) provides for judicial notice of a common fact of knowledge that does not require proof and it indeed may be argued that the fact of there being a meteorological report about the time that the sun arose in those two towns on that particular day is not -- does not require proof, yet the report itself is evidence that goes toward a fact that was litigated at trial, and in view of the Appellate Chamber, that evidence, the report, should have been submitted and could have been submitted to the trial Court at that time. Were we to allow Rule 94(A) to permit evidence to come in even though it is not necessary to provide further proof of that piece of evidence but evidence that was available at the time of trial, it would provide a way around 115 for pieces of evidence which although they themselves don't require proof, they are themselves evidence of a disputed fact. So the motion for judicial notice is rejected. Now, I wish to emphasise again, before we move on to the oral argument and the arrangements thereof, that under Rule 115, Friday, I believe, was the last day under the Rule that such motions could be filed. I am aware of the pending motions in the President's office and -- for access. I don't know what will come out of those, but I do wish to emphasise that barring extraordinary circumstances - whether or not that qualifies as an extraordinary circumstance, we will decide if it becomes necessary to decide - but apart from that, the Appeals Chamber will not entertain Rule 115 motions from this point onward. We have had, incidentally, over 30 of them so far, and I feel that closure -- we all feel that closure is coming due. With those out of the way, I would now like to discuss the forthcoming argument. Let me make a few preliminary remarks and then ask for the reactions of both the Prosecution and Defence counsel as to how we can make this a more expeditious process. We have three days, July 23rd through the 25th. We have, according to the maximum which we're able to squeeze out of those three days, a maximum of 18 hours for oral argument. That takes into account the necessary breaks for the translators and lunch. We have basically six separate appeals. We have the five appeals of the Prosecution, of the five -- I'm sorry, the five appeals of the five defendants and we have the Prosecution's one separate appeal. After today's discussion, and we'll go into that, the Appeals Chamber will, hopefully on Friday and certainly by Monday, issue a time schedule for the argument so that you'll all be clear, as you come into argument, whose going to argue at what time and about what. What I am hoping we can accomplish today is to agree on some practices that will make best use of both the Judges' and the counsels' time. Our legal officer, Mr. von Hebel, has written all of you a letter asking you to come today hopefully to propose some common issues on which one counsel could argue for more than one defendant. This is with a view to not having several Defence counsel arguing exactly the same argument. As you all know from reading the briefs, and I believe the Prosecution's brief specifically notes what it considers to be common arguments, but other defendants will quickly recognise that they have other common arguments with still other defendants, that it would be a waste of your time and a waste of our time for people to get up on the same side to give precisely the same league argument. And there so appear to be many such common arguments in these appeals. I myself have a list of some of the issues which appear to me to lend themselves to one argument on behalf of more than one defendant. However, I do stress I cannot force you to do that. I mean, there's no such thing as compulsory labour in this Tribunal. I can only urge you, on behalf of your own self, your own clients, and on behalf of the Judges' attention, that you try to, if you have not done so already, confer and to come up with some common issues that one of you can argue on behalf of more than one. And I would assure you that if you can agree on a joint presentation for some issues - "joint" doesn't mean one Defence counsel for all the other defendants but even one for two defendants or one for three defendants - we will be very careful to adjust the time accordingly so you will not suffer in any way by loss of time to agreeing to some such joint attention. Now, Mr. von Hebel asked you to come today prepared to see if there were any such common issues that you immediately identified, and I will at this time ask you, all of you, if that's so. After that, depending partially on what the answers are, I do have a list of issues I think that perhaps further consideration could be given to having a joint presentation, and I'm asking all of the counsel, but it's primarily Defence counsel here, obviously, to be in touch with Mr. von Hebel by the close of business on Wednesday, on Wednesday the 11th. Close of business is what time, Mr. von Hebel, for your office? 6.00 basically. In touch with him by fax or, if absolutely necessary by phone call, but fax is already better or a note, if you're here in The Hague, a letter. These do not have to be formal filings with the Registry. They are direct filings with Mr. von Hebel's office, in which you would apprise us of topics on which you and some, one, of the other counsels have agreed to present a joint argument, which counsel would argue on behalf of which defendants, and for you to make a suggested time limit for that joint argument. I'm aware that -- or you should be aware the Appeals Chamber will not necessarily be able to accommodate all of your requests, but we certainly will take them into consideration. So we hope that after this Status Conference is over, if there are any among the common issues which I will list which you can confer and come up with some joint presentations that you will be in touch with Mr. von Hebel by the end of Wednesday, and we'll get that into the schedule that we issue at the end of the week. All right. Let me -- there's no use in asking the Prosecutor, because the Prosecutor is unilateral in this sense as to whether or not there are any joint issues. The Prosecutor's brief identified issues that it considers to be common issue. Mr. Abell again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm so sorry to interrupt. I was only going to say that to some extent the exercise that Your Honour has mentioned, to some extent, at least, it has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Obviously Your Honour, from the sound of it, is going to give us a list of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- Which Your Honour has identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm going to listen to yours first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And if that's satisfactory, I may never have to get to mine, Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thus far --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You're not speaking -- let me just clarify. You're now speaking on behalf of some of the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I am indeed for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm -- obviously if anyone wants to add anything to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- about to say, they must have that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: But perhaps the main common issue is what has, I think, been referred to I think as the standard review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In other words, as we would put it, where does the evidential burden lie and the standard of proof to be applied. That appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That appears first on my list as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And ours. It is absolutely, we will submit, fundamental to the way that this appeal is approached. It has been agreed between the Defence, as I understand it that that argument will be taken on behalf of all of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- by Mr. William Clegg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's wonderful. That's good news indeed. Do you have a suggested time or -- you can do that to Mr. von Hebel later, because we'll have to balance, obviously, all the different time limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Of course, we will put it in writing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- the way Your Honour suggested, but I know that from discussions with Mr. Clegg, he was going to ask for two and a half hours in order to present that argument, but that would be on behalf of all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. Do you have other joint issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In relation to sentence, there is a joint issue perhaps, which is the impact of domestic sentencing law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- in the former Yugoslavia, as to tariff sentences, as it were. The effect that that -- the impact that that may have on the sentence appeals. And although it hasn't been decided who will deal with that yet, it is envisaged that that could be dealt with by one or perhaps -- perhaps two counsel on behalf of all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That will save a little time. The other joint or common matter doesn't affect my client, Vlatko Kupreskic, but as I'm on my feet, I'll deal with it. It's the cumulative conviction points. I'm aware of the recent ruling in the case of Jelisic. It's no part of my case, this, so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: -- I better not say too much more. One person - again, it's not been decided who - but one person will be pursuing that argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's good news. All of those three issues were certainly on my list. I hope that perhaps by Wednesday close of business counsel would be able to decide, in the case of the latter two, who would do the arguing. All right, Mr. Abell. Does that complete your -- that's a good report. How about other counsel? Mr. Radovic, there are many issues that you and Ms. Slokovic-Glumac have in common, and others. Do you have any suggestion for joint presentations? Either one of you is fine to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mrs. President. As we had joint Defence for the most part of the proceedings, we shall also treat these joint issues by splitting them between us. Mr. Radovic will take one part and I will take the other part. That is, the evidence that was produced and that we are challenging in our appeal will be analysed so that each one of us will take up one part of them and there will be no repetition. Of course, if there are some specific details relative to only one or the other accused, they will be tackled separately. We think that we shall need -- that each of us shall need about one hour and a half for the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Ms. Slokovic-Glumac. Do you think you will be in a position by Wednesday close of business to identify which issues each one of you will cover, or not? In your case, because your two arguments are so closely connected, I don't know that that's absolutely necessary, but it would be helpful if you did know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall do our best, but as I have said, we have not yet seen the Prosecutor's response, so that we simply do not know which are parts which are questionable, and that depends on that, how we shall react.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not only so that you have an opportunity to hear my voice, but I should also like to add a few sentences to contribute to this discussion, that is, to see how to best use the 18 hours envisaged for the closing arguments. At the outset, the position of the accused Santic and Josipovic was, insofar as the indictment and the charges were concerned, was practically the same. In other words, there are very many common issues and it is natural that one of us will address them all together. However, meanwhile, as you know, some changes took place, and our joint issues now boil down to legal issues, that is, the joinder of charges. Therefore, my colleague, who is speaking on behalf of -- who is here on behalf of Mr. Clegg, has already mentioned these cumulative charges and I suppose that we shall meet today to discuss which one of us will speak on the question of cumulation of charges. Now just one more thing. I should like to inform you how long I shall need for my presentation. I believe it will not go beyond one hour, even including the points on the cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have anything to add to this, Ms. Charbit?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Your Honour, only this: The merits of the appeal, Mr. Clegg has asked for one and a half hours to present his argument, and that's distinct from the two and a half hours for the argument already mentioned that may well be cumulative for other defendants. I can only indicate to the Court that in addition, he's asked for approximately 40 minutes for the rejoinder argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The rejoinder argument? In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHARBIT
utterances.text: Following the Prosecution response, he's asked for approximately 40 minutes for the reply to the Prosecution's argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand. All right. We have all those notations. Probably it would be useful if as many of you can put them in writing and just get them by note or fax to Mr. Clegg's office, but we do have them on the transcript even if you're not able to do that. We will get out a Scheduling Order, as I say, by the end of the week/beginning of next week. Now, you have been able to allay some of my apprehensions and encourage me by the progress you have made to joint presentations. However, if you will indulge me for just a few minutes, I am just going to list some of the other issues which I at least considered to be susceptible to joint presentation. In case any of you wish to think upon it some more, as I say, you have until Wednesday close of business to inform Mr. von Hebel. So I will just run down the list. I will not mention the ones that you've already agreed upon, but some of the other ones I've attempted, after reading the briefs, to indicate the particular defendants that would be raising the same issue. One of them is whether reliance for convictions may be had by the Trial Court on the basis of factual allegations that were not raised in the indictment. I'm putting the question not with any desire to indicate whether or not the Appellate Court at this time thinks that that's the proper formulation, but more in the terms of the way the appellants have formulated it. That was an issue raised by both Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and, I believe, by Mr. Josipovic as well. The failure to adequately define the charge of Prosecution. Now, that is raised by both Zoran and Mirjan, and I'm sure you've worked that out probably between yourself as to who will handle that. The same is true of the question raised by both Zoran and Mirjan dealing with the credibility of Witness H and the failure to call Witness SA, so I'll assume that you've worked that out between you. The credibility of Witness EE is an issue again which Mr. Josipovic and Mr. Santic had in common, and you've already alluded to the fact that you are working between yourselves on the allocation of issues. Which units were involved in the -- which military units were involved in the 16th of April attack on Ahmici is a question which is raised by both Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic and Mr. Josipovic. Now, on the sentencing issues, you've already mentioned one dealing with the practice of the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Let me mention a few others which seem to have been raised by more than one defendant and might also adapt themselves to joint presentation: The basic question of the standard of review in an appeal of sentence. I don't know whether that was intended to be included in the global issue on sentencing or not. Under what circumstances can new facts or mitigating circumstances be raised on appeal which were not put before the Trial Chamber? What is the standard of review of the Appellate Chamber for any new material which has come into the record with regard to sentencing? Did the Trial Court err in assessing the role of the various accused in the military or other hierarchies? Those are basically the issues which I saw. Some, or a few of them, might come within the orbit of those issues you've already identified as joint presentation. Others you might give further consideration to. But basically, if you'll give Mr. von Hebel by Wednesday night any other thoughts you have along these lines on joint presentation, then we will get the schedule out to you. You have already told me basically the time that you would like - it may not be possible to accommodate everybody - but the time that you would like. Now, do any of the Defence counsel who haven't already told me the amount of time that they think is necessary for them to present their case, are there any further thoughts on that from any of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure I actually -- when I rose to deal with the common issues, I'm not sure I dealt with what I was going to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So go ahead and deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In terms of presenting the merits of Vlatko Kupreskic's appeal, I would ask for 90 minutes for that, one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: In terms of the sentence aspects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I think that I might make clear here that except for those issues that have been pulled out for joint sentencing presentation, we would expect the Defence counsel to cover the sentencing within their main presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We weren't sure whether Your Honour was going to say separately or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I think we have so much division of time now that it's going to make more sense for the sentencing arguments to be made within the framework of the main appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Well, in which case I would revise my estimate. I was going to ask for 20 minutes for the sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So you get up to 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Your Honour's math is much sharper than mine. Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Anybody else have anything further to say on this? I do have one -- oh, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. There were one or two matters that I wanted to raise when my learned friends were mentioning about the time that they will spend on presenting their arguments -- actually, the joint issues. On the standard of review, it was mentioned that it would be done by Mr. Clegg and two and a half hours would be taken on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, he has asked for two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that it is the outer limit that he is asking for. What I want to mention is that this -- just a clarification, whether the standard of review that has been mentioned here is the standard review that is applicable to the main appeal, the substantive appeal, or whether it is together with the standard of review that will be in respect to the additional evidence that has been admitted, so it will have to be done jointly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand your question, and perhaps we can get that clarified by one of the Defence counsel now who participated in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe -- I certainly discussed it briefly with Mr. Clegg. It may be Ms. Charbit can help more, but I believe the intention was to deal with the issue globally within that two-and-a-half-hour framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So we would have, actually, three topics there: the standard of review for the evidence on the main appeal, anything additional that Mr. Clegg would like to present on standard of review for sentencing, and standard of review for additional material on 115. Thank you, Mr. Abell. Now, having gotten that somewhat clarified, what is the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I have one other matter to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, do you have -- okay. And then you will give us some estimate of the time you think you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will come to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If I may, with Your Honour's permission, mention: There was the other matter of cumulative convictions that was mentioned. Now, that is a ground that we have taken in our appeal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. There are actually two areas of cumulative conviction, in my understanding. One is the Prosecution's main appeal. That will be separated out in the oral argument. The Prosecution will have its appeal, the same way that the Defence counsel have their various appeals. Now, cumulative convictions that the Prosecution has not raised, cumulative conviction arguments that the Prosecution has not raised, have come up in the course of the appeals of several of the defendants. Those will be treated as part of the regular appellate arguments of those defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Those are the two matters I wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So I'm still waiting, Mr. Yapa, some notion of what kind of time frame you would envision for your separate Prosecution appeal and what kind of time frame you would envision. Plus, the question I had for you is: In terms of the five separate appeals raised by the five Defence counsel, does the Prosecution prefer to, at the end of each one of those appeals, have its time and then the Defence counsel have their time to come back, or would you rather have one big chunk of time at the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If Your Honour will bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. Our preference would be for the appellants to conclude their submissions and then we will make the response. It will be a response to arguments that what they place in their appeals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That would include the common issues as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: As well. As well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So you want -- just to clarify this: When your appeal comes up, you are obviously the appellant, you want a time for that, and you will tell me what your preference would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And then all of the appellants will present their arguments, you will present your global reply, and they will all have time to respond to your reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So if you'll give me two recommended preferred time slots for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: One thing which I can say straight away in respect of the response that we have to make to the appeal: We will work accordingly, because the time that they will take, it will be definitely lesser than the time that we will take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes. We would be here until Sunday if we -- an exact proportion of that amount.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: So what I can say is that it will be lesser than the time that they will take. But in respect of the appeal, the Prosecution appeal -- for the Prosecution appeal, what has been indicated to me, the person who has been entrusted to deal with it, is just 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's good news indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: And for the response, the reply to the response of the Defence, it will be -- if at all, it will be ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Okay. That's useful. I have been asked by my colleagues to make one general comment, which probably may not apply to any of you, but their experience with some other appeals is to advise counsel: Please do not read your argument. When you read your argument -- I know you're all experienced counsel and it's perhaps what we call preaching to the converted, but nonetheless, it not only, I think, detracts from the efficiency of the counsel; it makes it very hard for the Judges sitting for 18 almost straight hours if somebody is reading something. So we sincerely hope and urge that you will have a dialogue with us and not read from your appeal. Let me ask at this point: Apart from the outstanding motions and apart from the fact I will relay and show the transcript to my colleagues at Mr. Radovic's request, are there any other matters that you think need to be taken up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure that when I was last on my feet I indicated a time for what has been called -- using the terminology of the letter we received from Mr. von Hebel, it's been called rejoinder, our reply to the Prosecution's response. I would ask for 20 minutes to deal with that. Just a detail. We'll put it in the letter to Mr. von Hebel on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: No other matters that I can think of at the moment, Your Honour will be pleased to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, then, we will adjourn this Status Conference. I advise you all, because of the difficulties that various people have encountered in getting filings on time, to be aware, there will be decisions coming out on the 115 motions which are outstanding, decisions coming out on the access by the President, decisions by the President so that you can decide what to do with those decisions, and a schedule, either at the end of this week or Monday of next week, which will give you the -- so that if you don't receive them, you may want to make a phone call and make sure that they aren't sitting someplace where they are accessible. All right. Thank you very much. I appreciate especially the cooperative stance the Defence counsel have taken in trying to identify and move ahead on these joint submissions, and I look forward to seeing you again. I might add that at the end of the oral argument, we will have a very short regular Rule 65 bis Status Conference in order to accommodate the 120-day requirement when the accused defendants are here, and we'll do that at the very end of the argument. It shouldn't take more than a few minutes. Thank you.
